stops.name: The Querandí bring meat, and then withhold it
stops.campa: In the first weeks the Querandí of the open plain beyond the fort bring the starving Spaniards fish and the meat of the great deer of the pampa in exchange for trinkets, and for a season the two peoples eat side by side in something like peace. Then a Spanish demand for more than the hunters will give, and a beating given in answer to a refusal, break the arrangement past mending: the Querandí strike their tents and withdraw beyond the horizon, taking with them the only reliable meat the colony has ever had, and the siege, though no one yet calls it that, begins.

stops.name: The hunger begins
stops.campa: Without the Querandí's meat and with the ships' stores exhausted, the colony turns on the ground itself: parties dig for roots, net what fish the Riachuelo will give, range the reed-beds for birds' eggs. Ulrich Schmidl, a German soldier of the fleet who will outlast eighteen years here and write the only full chronicle of it, begins to keep the count of what a starving city will eat before it eats itself: first the rats and mice, then the snakes and every creeping thing, then, when even those fail, the leather of belts and saddle-tack.

stops.name: The boots eaten
stops.campa: By the deep of the austral winter there is nothing left that a stomach can be persuaded to hold: no rats, no mice, no snakes, no vermin of any kind to relieve the great need and the unheard-of misery, Schmidl writes, until the colonists come to eating their own shoes and every scrap of leather in the fort, boots, belts, harness, boiled soft or chewed raw. Men who came for gold gnaw their own footwear by the light of a fire built from the last dry planks of a beached ship, while the Querandí, unseen, watch the smoke from beyond the tall grass.
stops.quote: There remained neither rats, nor mice, nor snakes, nor any vermin to relieve us in our great need and unheard-of misery; we came to eating our shoes and all the leather.
stops.quote_source: Ulrich Schmidl, Viaje al Río de la Plata (Warhaftige Beschreibung, c. 1567)

stops.name: Three hanged for a stolen horse, and eaten in the night
stops.campa: Three Spaniards, driven past reason, steal and slaughter one of the colony's few remaining horses and are caught cooking it; Mendoza's officers try them and hang all three from the same gallows as a lesson to a city that cannot spare a single animal. That same night, other starving men, the chroniclers do not spare the detail, creep to the gibbet and cut meat from the thighs and arms of the three hanged corpses to carry home and eat. When word reaches the Crown, Charles V will rule that no sin was committed in such extremity: the first royal absolution of cannibalism in the history of the Indies.

stops.name: The siege tightens
stops.campa: With the Querandí now openly hostile and joined, the chroniclers say, by allied nations from farther on the plain, no foraging party can leave the palisade without arms, and few return without wounded. Mendoza, too sick to lead in the field, gives the command of the colony's defense increasingly to his brother Diego, admiral of the fleet and the ablest soldier left him; the fort's grain is measured by the handful and the horses, kept now under guard day and night, are worth more than any man's life among the starving garrison.

stops.name: Corpus Christi, the battle, and Diego's death
stops.campa: On the feast of Corpus Christi, Diego de Mendoza rides out with three hundred men and thirty horses to clear the Querandí from the country near the Laguna de Rocha, and is met instead by a confederated host the chroniclers number in the thousands. A boleadora brings down his horse; pinned beneath his fallen mount, Diego is run through by a Querandí lance, and with him fall his cousins Pedro and Luis de Benavídez and more than thirty other Spaniards. The ground where he dies will be called, from this day, the pago de la matanza, the killing-ground, and the name outlives every man who gave it.

stops.name: Corpus Christi, the fort raised upriver, the same feast day
stops.campa: On the very day his admiral dies on the pampa, far upriver on the Carcarañá, Juan de Ayolas, Mendoza's own steward, who inherited Osorio's place, raises a new fort beside the ruins Sebastián Caboto had left nine years before at Sancti Spíritu, and names it, by the same calendar's coincidence, Corpus Christi. Two forts of one name are born and die on one feast: one a grave on the killing-ground, the other a door, however narrow, toward the Andes and the rumored silver of Peru that will pull the whole colony's ambition steadily northward, away from the coast that bore it.

stops.name: Santa María del Buen Ayre, besieged and burned
stops.campa: On the feast of St John, nine days after the killing-ground, the Querandí and their allied nations close on the coastal fort in force, sending fire down on it with burning arrows; the palisade is breached, the storehouses and huts of wattle and thatch catch and burn, and four of the ships are lost at their moorings before the remnant garrison beats the assault back from the water's edge. What Mendoza founded in February as a city of two thousand is by midwinter a scorched stockade defended by starving men who sleep, when they sleep at all, with a weapon in hand and a horse saddled for flight.

stops.name: Buena Esperanza, Mendoza's own fort upriver
stops.campa: Sick past standing on his own feet, carried rather than riding, Mendoza nonetheless leads an expedition up the Paraná in the last days of September and founds, a few leagues from Ayolas's post, a fort he names, with the bitterest optimism the enterprise has left in it, Nuestra Señora de Buena Esperanza. Good Hope: for a passage west, for silver, for a harvest, for anything at all after eight months in which almost nothing his capitulación promised has come true. The fort will not outlast the year, but the name survives every ruin, as names do.

stops.name: The sickness wins; command passed to Ruiz Galán
stops.campa: By the new year Mendoza can no longer leave his cot; the disease taken at Rome ten years before has eaten through what strength the famine and the grief for Diego left him. Disheartened by every dispatch from upriver and unable to govern a colony he cannot even walk through, he names Juan de Ayolas his successor as captain-general and, under him, Francisco Ruiz Galán to hold Buenos Aires, and turns his whole remaining will toward a single decision: to go home to Spain, or to die trying.

stops.name: The departure, and the freeing of the herds
stops.campa: On the twenty-second of April the caravel Magdalena and the galleon Santantón stand out from the ruined fort with some hundred and fifty men and their broken adelantado aboard, bound for Spain and the physicians who might yet save him. Behind him, in the canon's own telling, the horses and cattle of his own armada are turned loose onto the grass rather than left to starve penned by a garrison too few to hold them: mares, stallions, cows loosed into a plain without wolves or lions to check them, the first free herd of a continent that has never had one.

stops.name: At sea, the will made near the equator
stops.campa: Off the coast, somewhere near the line where the two hemispheres meet, Mendoza, too weak now to leave his cabin, his whole body opened in sores, calls for paper and dictates his testament: pious bequests to the Church, provision for his servants and his nurse, and a last plea to the Crown to send men, food and arms to save the city he is leaving to die slowly behind him. He signs what he can still sign, and the ship sails on into the same ocean that carried him out two years before, older by a colony's worth of grief.
